attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, given as his argument.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'I'd argue' and the narrowed scope: filling Google's void by answering badly posed questions. 'I'd argue' states his position. It does not express probability. Causal is the right kind.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: it requires a query-understanding advantage linked to search-like adoption, and it does not require displacement of Google. The requirements correctly separate answer quality, formulation effort and adoption.

evidence.note: 2023 controlled study: ChatGPT users were faster, with no overall performance gap. ChatGPT did better on straightforward questions, not on poorly formulated ones. It does not test the proposed mechanism or show real-world adoption.

Semrush desktop clickstream data, US only, mostly after the post. It finds no drop in Google use after people adopt ChatGPT. That speaks to broad substitution, not to whether ChatGPT met an unmet need through query understanding.

reviews.rationale: No item ties an advantage on poorly formulated requests to ChatGPT adoption through April 2025. e1 tests different task types and finds no overall gap. e2 addresses aggregate substitution, which the contract says is not required. The packet does not settle the causal account.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The wording is broadly faithful. In context, though, 'hypergrowth markets' means growth engines that could sustain Big Tech and SaaS growth and valuations (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta). The bare proposition drops that sense.

contract.note: The contract treats ride-volume growth at two robotaxi operators as a hypergrowth market and sets no size minimum. The passage ties the claim to markets able to carry tech-industry growth and valuations. Counting small-scale usage growth as a refutation stretches the reading against him. The contract's own flags note this alternative reading.

evidence.note: Baidu's own disclosure: about 1.4M Apollo Go rides in Q1 2025, up 75% year on year. It shows fast usage growth at one firm, but not market revenue or scale relevant to tech-sector growth.

TechCrunch reports Pichai's figure of 200k weekly paid Waymo rides, 20x in two years, and Cruise's exit. This is fast usage growth at one firm. It does not establish a market large enough to replace Big Tech's growth engines.

reviews.rationale: On the contract's reading, the robotaxi ride growth would contradict the claim, but that reading is unfair. On the contextual reading (no other market able to sustain tech's growth), the packet has no evidence on aggregate revenue or scale, as its own gaps admit. The result is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, rebutting a critique he paraphrases. The rebuttal is his claim.

semantics.note: 'It sure seems like' is sarcastic emphasis after 'Source?'. It is not a probability hedge. The proposition omits his qualifier 'at least for the world outside China', which the contract does include.

contract.note: Reading 'costs' as total inference spending fits the context, which cites $6B. Reading 'effectively the entire userbase' as near-exclusive is the ordinary sense. Splitting the two clauses into a mixed result is fair.

evidence.note: Economist report: OpenAI expected 2025 inference costs to triple to $6bn. This supports rising total spending as reported and projected, not rising unit cost.

Court findings: Google's Mar 2025 estimates put ChatGPT at 1.2B daily queries against Meta AI 200M+, Gemini 140M, Grok 75M and others, and OpenAI's own US share estimate was about 85%. Rivals hold substantial activity, so usage is not near-exclusive.

reviews.rationale: The cost clause holds: reported total inference spending was expected to triple in 2025. The userbase clause fails: court-recorded estimates show substantial competing use, including Meta AI and Gemini, so OpenAI was the clear leader but not effectively the entire userbase.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithful: OpenAI, identified from the preceding text, takes most users and money because of media help. The language is firm.

contract.note: 'Most' as a majority and media as a material contributor are ordinary readings. The contract rightly leaves 'money' unspecified rather than picking a basis, and that blocks a full score.

evidence.note: Ramp data: 19.1% of US businesses use OpenAI versus 4.7% for Anthropic. This shows a lead in business adoption, not a majority of all users or money, and nothing about media effects.
2023 Tow Center measures of media coverage. It shows heavy attention but no causal effect on adoption, and it covers a different period.
a16z ties ChatGPT growth spikes to product launches. That is a competing explanation, but it does not rule out a media contribution.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no comparable market-wide user or money denominator for Q1 2025 and no study isolating the effect of media coverage. The items show OpenAI's lead, past media attention and a product-launch explanation, but none settles either the majority claim or the causal claim.
